slots.practicalActivity: Open a blank public repository under your own account for Project 1, write the one-paragraph project brief from the lesson (what document set you'll build the RAG assistant over, your stack, and what 'done' will look like) in its README, and add the one-sentence target-role choice (AI/RAG engineer, applied AI engineer with data, agentic/platform engineer, or 'undecided') next to it.
slots.deliverable: A created public GitHub repository with a README containing the Project 1 brief and your stated target-role sentence.

slots.practicalActivity: Create the real repository layout from the lesson (ingest/, index/, rag/, eval/, api/ folders), pick the actual real document set you'll build the RAG assistant over, commit the empty skeleton, and add the lesson's explicit out-of-scope list (no auth system, no multi-tenant isolation, no fine-tuning, no polished UI, no autoscaling) to your README before writing any pipeline code.
slots.deliverable: A committed repository skeleton with the five-folder layout, a chosen real document set, and a written out-of-scope list in the README.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the real loader and RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter chunker from the lesson over your own chosen document set, print the total chunk count, then read five consecutive chunks from one file and verify the 150-character overlap actually keeps every boundary-spanning sentence whole in at least one chunk.
slots.deliverable: Working ingestion and chunking code with a printed real chunk count and a documented check that overlap prevented a cut sentence from being lost.

slots.practicalActivity: Wire the lesson's three real steps (Qdrant query_points retrieval, numbered citable context assembly, and Claude Messages API generation) into one answer_question(question) function, run it against three real questions about your own document set, and check that each cited source actually contains the claim the model made.
slots.deliverable: A working answer_question function plus three real test runs with citation-accuracy notes for each question.

slots.practicalActivity: Build your own real 15-20 question eval set from your document set, run the lesson's two real measurements (retrieval recall@5 and LLM-as-judge generation scoring) to get a baseline, then change exactly one tuning lever (chunk size, top-k, or add a re-ranking pass) and record whether the numbers actually moved.
slots.deliverable: A recorded baseline recall@5 and judge score, plus a post-tuning re-measurement showing the real before/after numbers.

slots.practicalActivity: Wrap your answer_question function in the lesson's FastAPI /ask endpoint, build the Docker image from the real Dockerfile, run it locally with your Anthropic API key passed as an environment variable (never baked into the image), hit /ask with a real curl call, and confirm the response includes citations.
slots.deliverable: A running containerized RAG API service with a captured real curl response showing citations, plus an updated README with architecture, eval numbers, and tradeoffs.

slots.practicalActivity: Project 1 build lab: finish the RAG knowledge assistant end to end as a complete portfolio piece — push the containerized service, finalize the README's architecture, eval-numbers, and tradeoffs sections, and if your target role points to RAG/AI engineering, add one additional polish pass now (a larger eval set, a sharper README, or a short recorded demo walkthrough) before moving to Project 2.
slots.deliverable: A fully pushed, portfolio-ready Project 1 repository with a finished README and, if emphasized, one real polish addition.

slots.practicalActivity: Scope your own real Project 2: pick a real SQL database with at least two or three related tables (or stand one up locally with a public sample dataset) and a real external API that adds something the database doesn't have, then write down three to five real questions a user would actually ask that need both.
slots.deliverable: A written Project 2 scope naming the chosen database, the chosen API, and three to five real test questions requiring both.

slots.practicalActivity: Stand up your real Project 2 database, create a dedicated read-only role scoped only to the tables your project needs, connect to it from code using parameterized queries (never string-concatenated SQL), set a statement timeout, and confirm the role's connection actually fails if you manually try an INSERT against it.
slots.deliverable: Working parameterized, read-only database connection code plus a confirmed failed-INSERT test proving the role can't write.

slots.practicalActivity: Define the real run_sql_query tool for your own database, write a schema-aware system prompt describing your actual tables and columns, wire up the lesson's validate_sql() function, and run your three to five test questions end to end, confirming each produces a validated SELECT before touching your read-only connection.
slots.deliverable: Working natural-language-to-SQL tool-calling code with validation, and captured real validated-SQL output for all three to five test questions.

lessons.title: Combining SQL Results With API Data

slots.practicalActivity: Add your real external API as a second tool alongside run_sql_query, implement the lesson's retry/backoff pattern for the API call, add deduplication across rows to avoid the N+1 trap, and run the one test question from your scope that needs both the database and the API, confirming Claude's final answer correctly combines both results.
slots.deliverable: Working multi-tool code combining a real SQL result with a real API call, with a captured end-to-end answer for the combined test question.

slots.practicalActivity: Write your Project 2 README using the lesson's five-part structure (problem, architecture, safety decisions, demo, known limitations — written as specifically as the lesson's example), rehearse a 3-5 minute walkthrough covering all five parts, and get it in front of one other person for real feedback.
slots.deliverable: A finished five-part Project 2 README plus notes from one real feedback session on a rehearsed walkthrough.

slots.practicalActivity: Project 2 build lab: finish the AI data analyst end to end as a complete portfolio piece — push the finished code and README, verify every one of your three to five test questions actually runs end to end against your real database and API, and if your target role points to applied/data-focused AI engineering, add one additional polish pass (a deployed API behind FastAPI/Docker, or a larger test-question set) before moving to Project 3.
slots.deliverable: A fully pushed, portfolio-ready Project 2 repository with every test question verified working end to end.

lessons.title: Project 3 Kickoff
lessons.chapterTitle: Project 3 — Tool-Using Agent With Human Approval

slots.practicalActivity: Scope your own real Project 3: choose at least one tool with a real, hard-to-reverse consequence (sending a message, modifying a record, placing an order) plus one or two lower-risk read-only tools, and write down the plausible real reason a human needs to be in the loop for the high-risk tool (cost, reputational risk, irreversibility, or compliance exposure).
slots.deliverable: A written Project 3 scope naming your chosen tools, their risk levels, and the specific real reason the high-risk tool needs human approval.

lessons.title: Designing the Tool Set
lessons.chapterTitle: Project 3 — Tool-Using Agent With Human Approval

slots.practicalActivity: Write the real Messages API tool definitions for your own two to three Project 3 tools, following the worked look_up_order/issue_refund example's description discipline including an explicit 'when NOT to use this' clause, then classify each tool's risk tier and requires_approval flag in a short table.
slots.deliverable: Real JSON tool-definition schemas for two to three tools plus a completed risk-tier/requires_approval table.

lessons.title: Building the Approval Workflow
lessons.chapterTitle: Project 3 — Tool-Using Agent With Human Approval

slots.practicalActivity: Implement the lesson's real dispatcher (handle_tool_use) for your requires_approval tool, build a minimal reviewer interface (a CLI prompt is fine), and confirm both paths work correctly — an approved call that actually executes and sends a real tool_result, and a rejected call that sends an is_error: true result with an instructive message Claude can act on.
slots.deliverable: Working approval-dispatcher code with captured real transcripts of both an approved and a rejected tool call.

lessons.title: Adding Security & Logging
lessons.chapterTitle: Project 3 — Tool-Using Agent With Human Approval

slots.practicalActivity: Add a validate_refund_input-style function for your own requires_approval tool that re-derives its critical value from your own data instead of trusting the model's claim, and add audit logging covering all four real outcomes: validation failure, rejection, approval, and execution.
slots.deliverable: Working input-validation code plus captured real audit-log entries covering all four outcomes.

lessons.title: Deploying the Agent
lessons.chapterTitle: Project 3 — Tool-Using Agent With Human Approval

slots.practicalActivity: Write the real Dockerfile for your Project 3 agent, move its pending-approval store and audit log from memory/stdout into a real database table, run the container locally with secrets passed as environment variables (never baked into the image), and confirm a container restart doesn't lose a pending approval.
slots.deliverable: A working containerized agent with durable pending-approval and audit-log storage, verified to survive a real restart.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up & Presentation
lessons.chapterTitle: Project 3 — Tool-Using Agent With Human Approval

slots.practicalActivity: Update your Project 3 README with the adapted five-part structure, and this time actually demonstrate — recorded or described — the rejected path: trigger your sensitive tool, reject it live, show Claude's real response to the is_error result, then run it again and approve it, capturing both real outcomes.
slots.deliverable: A finished Project 3 README plus captured real transcripts of both the rejected-path and approved-path demos.

slots.practicalActivity: Project 3 build lab — the most substantial build in this course: finish the tool-using agent as a complete, deployed, portfolio-grade system. Push the containerized service with durable state, re-verify the full approve/reject round trip against the live deployment (not just a local run), and write the honest, specific known-limitations section for your own build following the lesson's example. With all three capstone projects now complete, do one additional deep polish pass (a sharper README, a recorded demo, a larger eval set) on whichever project matches your target role.
slots.deliverable: A fully deployed, portfolio-ready Project 3 agent with a verified live approve/reject round trip and a written known-limitations section, plus one real polish addition to your chosen flagship project.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the action + artifact + framework pattern from the lesson, write one real resume bullet for a deliverable from each of your three capstone projects, including a real metric or link you could actually defend if asked about it for each one.
slots.deliverable: Three real action + artifact + framework resume bullets, one per capstone project, each with a real metric or link.

slots.practicalActivity: Write (or rewrite) the README for your strongest capstone project using the lesson's five-part structure (one-sentence description, architecture diagram, demo link, eval results, key design decisions), including a real eval number and a tested demo link, or outline the three things a 3-minute demo recording would show if you don't have one yet.
slots.deliverable: A finished five-part README for your strongest capstone project, or a written three-point demo-recording outline if no recording exists yet.

lessons.title: System Design Questions for AI Roles

slots.practicalActivity: Pick three interview questions from the lesson (one from each of three categories) and answer each out loud in under 90 seconds using the name-the-tradeoff method, then pick one system-design prompt ('design a RAG assistant for X' or 'design an agent with human approval for Y') and write a full four-part answer (requirements, architecture, tradeoffs, failure modes) from scratch, recording yourself for both if you can.
slots.deliverable: Three recorded or written tradeoff-method interview answers plus one complete four-part system-design answer.

slots.practicalActivity: Using at least two source types from the lesson's table (an aggregated salary site, government labor data, or live job postings) and at least two AI-role title variants, research a real compensation range — base and equity component if relevant — for your actual target experience level and company stage, and write down the low end, the high end, your sources, and the company stage most postings reflected.
slots.deliverable: A written, sourced compensation range (low end, high end, sources, company stage) for your real target role.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course — and the entire AI Engineer path — a student has three real, deployed, evaluated flagship projects (a production RAG knowledge assistant with measured retrieval and faithfulness scores, an AI data analyst running safe natural-language-to-SQL against a real database plus live API enrichment, and a tool-using agent with a working human-approval checkpoint, audit logging, and security controls) along with a tailored resume, a presentable GitHub portfolio, and a proven method for answering AI engineering interview and system-design questions.
